references.title: One shopping budget
mapping: A fixed budget makes the two feasible baskets mutually exclusive.
Choosing basket A forgoes the value of the best feasible alternative B, not the sum of all alternatives.
references.limitation: Prices alone do not determine personal benefit; money spent and opportunity cost need not coincide.
references.diagnostic: If three baskets are possible, do we add the benefits of both rejected baskets?
references.transfer: A free evening permits either a paid shift worth 70 or a class worth 90 to you. What is the opportunity cost of the class?

references.title: An evening with two plans
mapping: An overlapping schedule prevents attending both plans.
The benefit of the highest-valued foregone feasible plan is the opportunity cost.
references.limitation: Schedules can sometimes be rearranged; the example assumes the conflict is unavoidable.
references.diagnostic: Does a zero admission price make an activity costless?
references.transfer: A workshop uses a room that could otherwise earn 120 in rent. Identify the foregone benefit.

references.title: Using the last ingredients
mapping: The same scarce ingredients can make one of two dishes.
Using them for one dish forgoes the best alternative use.
references.limitation: Ingredients may be divisible and tastes differ; this example treats each complete meal as indivisible.
references.diagnostic: Is the cost necessarily what was paid for the ingredients last month?
references.transfer: An unused machine can produce 8 chairs or 5 tables today. Explain what is forgone by producing tables.

references.title: Original story: the cooperative room
mapping: In the hypothetical final chapter, the cooperative assigns its only room to free classes.
The best rejected feasible use was a rental worth 200, making that benefit forgone.
references.limitation: A fictional decision does not establish real costs or justify prioritizing money over other benefits.
references.diagnostic: Which rejected use determines the opportunity cost?
references.transfer: A public hall can host one event or be rented. Describe the relevant alternative before calculating cost.

references.title: One additional meal portion
mapping: One extra portion changes total ingredient cost by an incremental amount.
Choose the extra portion when its additional benefit exceeds its additional cost; exclude costs unchanged by that choice.
references.limitation: Discrete portions and capacity limits matter; this is not a continuous optimization model.
references.diagnostic: Should unchanged rent be added again when deciding to cook one extra portion?
references.transfer: A printer pays a fixed setup fee and 3 per extra poster. A buyer offers 5 for one more. Evaluate only the increment.

references.title: One additional purchase
mapping: Compare total benefit and total cost before and after adding one unit.
The differences, rather than average totals, govern the incremental purchase.
references.limitation: The extra unit may have a different benefit from earlier units; quantity discounts must be accounted for explicitly.
references.diagnostic: Can an average unit cost replace the cost of the next unit?
references.transfer: An extra hour of practice adds benefit valued at 12 and fatigue valued at 15. Compare the increment.

references.title: The final leg of a trip
mapping: Compare the additional minutes saved by a detour with its additional fuel cost.
Time and money must be converted to an explicitly stated common valuation before subtraction.
references.limitation: Travel time is uncertain and valuations are personal; the example is not a transport recommendation.
references.diagnostic: Can five minutes and five currency units be subtracted without a conversion?
references.transfer: An extra machine hour yields 18 in output and costs 21 in power and wear. Should it run?

references.title: An extra study interval
mapping: A further study interval can add less learning than the preceding interval.
Compare the benefit and cost of that next interval, holding previous work fixed.
references.limitation: Learning is difficult to value precisely; this only illustrates the decision structure.
references.diagnostic: Does the value of all past study tell us the value of the next interval?
references.transfer: A gardener considers one extra hour of watering with benefit 9 and cost 11. Decide using differences.

references.title: Drawing from a known bag
mapping: Conditioning on a bag or subset restricts the denominator to that group.
Count target outcomes within the restricted group, divided by all outcomes in that group.
references.limitation: Uniform drawing is assumed; unequal selection weights need a different calculation.
references.diagnostic: After learning the bag is blue, should objects in the red bag remain in the denominator?
references.transfer: A club has 30 evening members, 12 of whom cycle. Among evening members, what fraction cycle?

references.title: Rain among cloudy days
mapping: Restrict a historical table to days recorded as cloudy.
The fraction of rainy days in that subset estimates rain conditional on cloud in that dataset.
references.limitation: A small historical sample need not predict future weather; conditioning is not causation.
references.diagnostic: Is rain given cloud necessarily equal to cloud given rain?
references.transfer: Among 40 packages sent express, 6 arrived late. Find the observed late proportion conditional on express.

references.title: A card after its color is known
mapping: Knowing a card is red removes black cards from the possible outcomes.
A red target category is counted within the remaining red cards.
references.limitation: The deck must have known counts and a uniform draw; this is not a strategy for gambling.
references.diagnostic: Does learning the color physically change which card was drawn?
references.transfer: Of 24 students who chose art, 9 also chose music. Find the proportion choosing music conditional on art.

references.title: Orders among members
mapping: Filter a hypothetical order table to members before counting express delivery.
The member count, rather than all customers, is the conditional denominator.
references.limitation: A purchase context requires a supplied table; liking shopping does not imply statistical knowledge.
references.diagnostic: Which group belongs in the denominator for express delivery given membership?
references.transfer: Among 50 manufactured parts passing inspection A, 45 pass B. Estimate B conditional on A in that batch.

references.title: Two draws with replacement
mapping: Replacement and reshuffling restore the same deck distribution before the next draw.
Under uniform independent draws, the first outcome does not change the probability of the second; multiply probabilities for the joint event.
references.limitation: Without replacement the events can be dependent; physical shuffling quality is an assumption.
references.diagnostic: What changes if the first card is not replaced?
references.transfer: Two independently checked devices each work with probability 0.9. Find the probability both work.

references.title: Draws from separate bags
mapping: One uniform draw from each separately prepared bag leaves the second bag unchanged.
With independent randomization the joint event probability is the product of the two marginal probabilities.
references.limitation: Separate containers alone do not guarantee independent randomization; shared hidden causes can induce dependence.
references.diagnostic: Does a different container by itself prove independence?
references.transfer: Two independent fair spinners each have four equal sectors. Find the probability both show sector 1.

references.title: Two nearby weather reports
mapping: A shared weather system can affect both reports.
If observing one changes the probability of the other, independence fails and unconditional probabilities cannot simply be multiplied.
references.limitation: Correlation and geographic proximity do not quantify the dependence; a joint model or data is needed.
references.diagnostic: Would different town names suffice to justify multiplying rain probabilities?
references.transfer: Two shops share one unreliable electricity line. Explain why separate premises do not establish independent outages.

references.title: Delays on a shared route
mapping: Two vehicles can be delayed by the same road closure.
The shared event changes conditional delay probabilities, so independence needs justification.
references.limitation: Different routes can still share weather or demand shocks; this is a conceptual counterexample.
references.diagnostic: If one vehicle is delayed, could that change what you infer about the other?
references.transfer: Two online services share a server. Explain why separate names do not imply independent failure.
